questions.q: Which historical feature is classically elicited first when taking the history of a localized swelling?
options: When and how the lump was first noticed
Whether the lump transilluminates
Presence of regional lymphadenopathy on palpation
Consistency of the deeper margins
questions.explain: History of a swelling begins with duration and mode of onset (when and how it was first noticed, such as incidentally during bathing or following trauma), followed by changes in size, pain, multiplicity, and systemic symptoms.

open.q: What is the very first specific question asked when taking the history of presenting complaint for a patient with a lump?
accept: When and how the lump was first noticed
When the lump was first noticed

questions.q: Why should the temperature of a localized swelling be assessed using the dorsal surface of the examiner's fingers?
options: The dorsal skin is thinner and more sensitive to subtle temperature differences
The palmar surface has fewer mechanoreceptors
The dorsal surface prevents bacterial contamination of the lesion
The palmar skin conducts heat away too rapidly
questions.explain: The skin on the dorsum of the fingers and hand is thinner with less keratin and subcutaneous fat, making its thermoreceptors more sensitive to localized warmth indicative of acute inflammation or hypervascularity.

open.q: Why is the back of the fingers preferred over the palmar surface when checking the local temperature of a swelling?
accept: The dorsal skin is thinner and more sensitive to temperature changes
Thinner skin on the dorsum is more sensitive to warmth
Greater thermal sensitivity of the thinner dorsal skin

questions.q: Which bedside palpation sign is positive when pressing the centre of a soft lump causes its edges to bulge outward in two perpendicular planes?
options: Fluctuation
Indentation
Slip sign
Expansile pulsation
questions.explain: Fluctuation (Paget's sign) demonstrates fluid or semi-fluid content within a cyst or abscess; pressing one pole displaces fluid, causing a watching finger at the opposite pole to lift in two planes at right angles.

open.q: Name the clinical sign elicited in two perpendicular planes that confirms a swelling contains fluid or soft semi-solid material.

questions.q: What is the clinical significance of a positive slip sign when examining a subcutaneous swelling?
options: The rounded margin slips away from under the examining finger, characteristic of a lipoma
The swelling empties completely on pressure and refills slowly, characteristic of a cavernous haemangioma
The swelling disappears upon coughing, characteristic of a reducible hernia
The overlying skin cannot be pinched free, characteristic of an epidermoid cyst
questions.explain: A lipoma has smooth, lobulated, rounded edges that slip out from beneath the palpating finger when gentle pressure is applied to its margin (the slip sign). Emptying on pressure describes compressibility.

open.q: Which benign mesenchymal tumour is classically identified on palpation by a positive slip sign at its lobulated edge?

questions.q: How do you clinically differentiate a swelling with expansile pulsation from one with transmitted pulsation?
options: Opposing fingers move apart with expansile pulsation but together with transmitted pulsation
Expansile pulsation disappears when the patient holds their breath
Transmitted pulsation produces a machinery murmur
Expansile pulsation occurs only with muscle contraction
questions.explain: In an aneurysm (expansile pulsation), each systole expands the wall radially in all directions, pushing two laterally placed fingers apart. A mass lying over an artery receives transmitted pulsation, lifting both fingers parallel to each other.

open.q: When placing two fingers on opposite sides of a pulsatile lump, how does the movement of the fingers distinguish an aneurysm from a mass overlying a major artery?
accept: The fingers are pushed apart in an aneurysm but move upward together in transmitted pulsation
Fingers separate in expansile pulsation and move in the same direction in transmitted pulsation

questions.q: Which of the following swellings characteristically demonstrates brilliant transillumination on pen-torch examination in a darkened room?
options: Vaginal hydrocele
Lipoma
Epidermoid cyst
Cold tuberculous abscess
questions.explain: Transillumination occurs when light passes through clear fluid (such as in a vaginal hydrocele, cystic hygroma, or meningocele). Thick sebaceous material in an epidermoid cyst, pus, blood, and solid fat do not transilluminate.

open.q: Why does a vaginal hydrocele transilluminate brightly whereas a sebaceous cyst does not?
accept: A hydrocele contains clear serous fluid that transmits light, while a sebaceous cyst contains thick opaque sebum
Clear fluid allows light transmission whereas thick keratinous debris blocks light

questions.q: What is the key clinical distinction between a reducible swelling and a compressible swelling?
options: A compressible swelling refills on release; a reducible one needs a manoeuvre to reappear
A reducible swelling never changes with posture
A compressible swelling always has a cough impulse
A reducible swelling contains only arterial blood
questions.explain: Compressible swellings (like haemangiomas or lymphangiomas) are squeezed empty by external pressure and immediately refill upon release. Reducible swellings (like hernias) are pushed back into a body cavity and stay reduced until gravity or raised intra-abdominal pressure forces them out again.

open.q: How does the refilling behaviour after releasing manual pressure differentiate a compressible swelling from a reducible swelling?
accept: A compressible swelling refills immediately on release of pressure, whereas a reducible swelling stays reduced until an expulsive force like coughing occurs
Compressible swellings refill spontaneously upon release while reducible swellings require coughing or straining

questions.q: An epidermoid (sebaceous) cyst is characteristically tethered to which anatomical layer?
options: Overlying epidermis via a central punctum
Deep fascia of the underlying skeletal muscle
Periosteum of the adjacent bone
Subcutaneous fat only without skin attachment
questions.explain: Because an epidermoid cyst arises from blocked pilosebaceous follicles or implanted epidermal cells, it is fixed to the overlying skin (often showing a visible punctum) while remaining freely mobile over deeper structures.

open.q: Which anatomical structure is an epidermoid cyst characteristically attached to, preventing the skin from being pinched over its summit?

questions.q: A lump on the anterior thigh becomes less prominent and completely immobile when the patient contracts the quadriceps femoris muscle. In which anatomical plane does the lump lie?
options: Intramuscular or subfascial plane
Subcutaneous plane
Intradermal plane
Epidermal plane
questions.explain: When an underlying muscle contracts, the taut deep fascia flattens and obscures subfascial or intramuscular swellings, while fixing intramuscular lumps. Subcutaneous lumps become more prominent and remain mobile when the muscle is tensed.

open.q: If a limb lump becomes less prominent and restricted in mobility when the underlying muscle contracts, where is the lump located relative to the deep fascia?
accept: Deep to the deep fascia or within the muscle

questions.q: Which of the following defines an ulcer pathologically and clinically?
options: A break in the continuity of an epithelial surface
A blind-ending tract lined by granulation tissue opening onto a surface
An abnormal communication between two epithelial-lined surfaces
A localized collection of pus within a newly formed cavity
questions.explain: An ulcer is a discontinuity or break in an epithelial surface (skin or mucous membrane). A blind-ending tract is a sinus, and an abnormal tract connecting two epithelial surfaces is a fistula.

open.q: Give the concise clinical definition of an ulcer.
accept: A break in the continuity of an epithelial surface
Discontinuity of skin or mucous membrane
Loss of continuity of an epithelial lining

questions.q: Which ulcer edge morphology is classically seen in a rodent ulcer (basal cell carcinoma)?
options: Rolled, pearly edge with telangiectasia
Undermined edge
Punched-out edge
Sloping edge
questions.explain: Basal cell carcinoma displays a raised, pearly, rolled edge traversed by fine telangiectatic vessels. Undermined edges occur in tuberculosis, punched-out edges in syphilis or neuropathic ulcers, and sloping edges in healing venous ulcers.

open.q: Describe the characteristic edge appearance of a basal cell carcinoma (rodent) ulcer.

questions.q: An ulcer with a thin, bluish, undermined edge is most characteristic of which underlying pathology?
options: Tuberculosis
Squamous cell carcinoma
Basal cell carcinoma
Healing venous ulcer
questions.explain: In tuberculous ulcers, subcutaneous tissue is destroyed more rapidly than the overlying skin, leaving a thin, overhanging, bluish undermined edge. Pressure sores also develop undermined edges due to deep tissue necrosis.

open.q: Which chronic granulomatous infection classically produces an ulcer with an undermined, bluish edge?

questions.q: Which type of ulcer characteristically possesses a raised, everted (rolled-out) edge and an indurated base?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma
Syphilitic gummatous ulcer
Ischaemic arterial ulcer
Tropical phagedenic ulcer
questions.explain: Rapid malignant proliferation at the margins heaps up tissue outward over the surrounding normal skin, creating the classic raised, everted edge of squamous cell carcinoma (including Marjolin ulcer in an old burn scar).

open.q: What edge morphology is diagnostic on inspection of a squamous cell carcinoma ulcer?

questions.q: What is the key anatomical difference between the floor and the base of an ulcer?
options: The floor is the visible ulcer surface; the base is the underlying tissue felt on palpation
The base is inspected; the floor is assessed only by biopsy
The floor is surrounding skin; the base is exudate
Only malignant ulcers have a base
questions.explain: The floor of an ulcer is what you see (e.g., pink granulation tissue, slough, or wash-leather slough), while the base is the underlying tissue supporting the ulcer that you palpate for induration and deep fixation.

open.q: Distinguish between the floor of an ulcer and the base of an ulcer during physical examination.
accept: The floor is the visible exposed surface seen on inspection, while the base is the underlying tissue felt on palpation
Floor is inspected visually and base is palpated beneath the ulcer

questions.q: A 55-year-old diabetic man presents with a painless, deep, punched-out ulcer over the plantar surface of the first metatarsal head surrounded by thick hyperkeratotic callus. What is the primary mechanism?
options: Peripheral sensory neuropathy with repetitive mechanical pressure
Acute arterial embolism of the dorsalis pedis artery
Deep venous valvular incompetence of the perforators
Cutaneous basal cell carcinoma invasion
questions.explain: Painless punched-out ulcers over weight-bearing pressure points (such as the metatarsal heads or heel) surrounded by callus are classic neuropathic (trophic) ulcers caused by loss of protective pain sensation in diabetes or leprosy.

open.q: What type of ulcer presents as a painless, punched-out lesion surrounded by thick callus over the plantar metatarsal head in a patient with peripheral neuropathy?

questions.q: Where is a venous ulcer most commonly situated on the lower limb?
options: Over the medial malleolus (gaiter area)
Over the lateral malleolus and dorsum of the foot
At the tips of the toes
Over the plantar surface of the heel
questions.explain: Venous ulcers occur in the gaiter region, predominantly just superior to the medial malleolus where medial ankle perforating veins are located, accompanied by haemosiderin pigmentation and lipodermatosclerosis. Arterial ulcers favour the toes, heel, and lateral malleolus.

open.q: What is the classic anatomical site on the lower leg for a chronic venous ulcer?
accept: Gaiter area around the medial malleolus

questions.q: Which three concentric zones are visible on inspection of a healing ulcer with a sloping edge?
options: Inner red granulation, middle blue-white epithelium and outer white scar
Inner black eschar, middle pus and outer nodules
Inner slough, middle undermining and outer hyperkeratosis
Inner telangiectasia, middle slough and outer lymphoedema
questions.explain: A healthy healing ulcer has a gently sloping edge showing three zones from centre to periphery: red vascular granulation tissue (floor), a bluish-pink zone of migrating single-layer epithelium, and an outer white zone of mature stratified squamous epithelium.

open.q: Name the three colour zones seen from the centre outward in a healing ulcer with a sloping edge.
accept: Red granulation tissue, blue regenerating epithelium, and white mature scar

questions.q: What does induration at the edge and base of a chronic ulcer strongly suggest on palpation?
options: Malignant infiltration or chronic granulomatous fibrosis
Acute bacterial cellulitis only
Superficial epidermal abrasion
Purely venous congestion without tissue change
questions.explain: Induration (woody hardness felt on gently pinching the edge and base of an ulcer) is a hallmark of malignant invasion (such as squamous cell carcinoma) or dense chronic fibrosis (such as a syphilitic chancre).

open.q: What clinical finding on palpation of an ulcer's edge and base raises strong suspicion of malignancy?
accept: Hardness or induration of the edge and base

questions.q: Which ulcer classically features a grey-yellow adherent 'wash-leather' slough on its floor?
options: Syphilitic gummatous ulcer
Rodent ulcer
Venous stasis ulcer
Aphthous ulcer
questions.explain: A tertiary syphilitic gumma breaks down to form a deep, painless, punched-out ulcer with a characteristic greyish-yellow, rubbery 'wash-leather' slough on its floor.

open.q: Which infective ulcer is classically described as having a punched-out edge and a 'wash-leather' slough on its floor?

questions.q: Why must the regional lymph nodes always be examined after inspecting and palpating any ulcer or lump?
options: To detect secondary infection (reactive lymphadenitis) or lymphatic metastasis
To assess arterial perfusion to the ulcer bed
To determine the depth of underlying muscle invasion
To confirm whether the lesion transilluminates
questions.explain: Examination of any lump or ulcer is incomplete without palpating its draining lymph node basin; soft, tender, mobile nodes suggest secondary infection, whereas hard, fixed, non-tender nodes suggest metastatic spread.

open.q: What are the two main pathological processes indicated by enlargement of regional lymph nodes draining an ulcer?

questions.q: Which clinical sign on examination of a sinus opening suggests an underlying retained foreign body or necrotic bone sequestrum?
options: Exuberant, pouting red granulation tissue protruding from the sinus orifice
A completely dry, healed epithelialized dimple
Bright red arterial bleeding synchronized with the radial pulse
Transparent serous fluid that transilluminates
questions.explain: Pouting granulation tissue heaped up around a sinus opening (proud flesh) is a classic sign of persistent foreign material (such as a non-absorbable suture) or dead bone (sequestrum in chronic osteomyelitis) preventing closure.

open.q: What visual appearance at the external opening of a sinus points toward a retained foreign body or bone sequestrum?
accept: Exuberant granulation tissue protruding from the opening
Heaped-up granulation tissue at the orifice

questions.q: Which physical sign differentiates a true cyst from a solid soft-tissue tumour on palpation?
options: Positive fluctuation test in two perpendicular planes
Lobulated surface with a positive slip sign
Hard, irregular, fixed margins
Presence of an audible systolic bruit
questions.explain: A cyst is a fluid-filled sac lined by epithelium or endothelium that yields a positive fluctuation sign in two planes at right angles (unless very tense or deep), whereas solid tumours do not fluctuate.

open.q: What bedside palpation test confirms that a superficial swelling is cystic rather than solid?

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with a smooth, firm, non-tender 3 cm spherical swelling on his upper back. The overlying skin cannot be pinched free at the summit, and a dark central punctum is visible. What is the diagnosis?
options: Epidermoid (sebaceous) cyst
Subcutaneous lipoma
Dermoid cyst
Neurofibroma
questions.explain: An intradermal/subcutaneous spherical swelling tethered to the skin with a central punctum is diagnostic of an epidermoid cyst. Dermoid cysts occur along embryonic fusion lines and lack a punctum, while lipomas allow the skin to be pinched freely.

open.q: A smooth, spherical lump on the back is tethered to the skin and exhibits a dark central punctum. What is the diagnosis?

questions.q: What is the clinical term for indentation of a firm swelling upon sustained fingertip pressure, classically seen in an epidermoid cyst or faecal mass?
options: Moulding (indentation)
Fluctuation
Crepitus
Ballottement
questions.explain: Moulding or indentation occurs when firm pressure leaves a persistent dent in thick putty-like contents (such as inspissated keratin in a large epidermoid cyst or impacted faeces in the colon).

open.q: What is the clinical sign where firm fingertip pressure leaves a persistent dent in a swelling filled with putty-like material?

questions.q: A 42-year-old farmer develops a rapidly growing, foul-smelling, indurated ulcer with raised everted edges within a 20-year-old untreated burn scar on his lower leg. What is this lesion called?
options: Marjolin ulcer
Curling ulcer
Cushing ulcer
Rodent ulcer
questions.explain: Marjolin ulcer is a well-differentiated, aggressive squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic scar, burn wound, venous ulcer, or chronic osteomyelitis sinus tract. Curling ulcers follow severe burns in the duodenum.

open.q: Name the malignant ulcer that arises within a chronic burn scar or long-standing venous ulcer.
